question.prompt: You are playing a game. A \(2\times 1\) rectangle covers two adjacent squares (oriented either horizontally or vertically) of a \(3\times 3\) grid of squares, but you are not told which two squares are covered. Your goal is to find at least one square that is covered by the rectangle. A “turn” consists of you guessing a square, after which you are told whether that square is covered by the hidden rectangle. What is the minimum number of turns you need to ensure that at least one of your guessed squares is covered by the rectangle?

solutions.title: Separate candidates, then color
solutions.explanation:
Four possible rectangle positions can be chosen without sharing any squares. This gives a lower bound on the number of guesses needed.

Label the squares by
\[
\begin{matrix}
1&2&3\\
4&5&6\\
7&8&9
\end{matrix}
\]
Consider the four rectangle positions covering
\[
(1,2),\quad(4,5),\quad(7,8),\quad(3,6).
\]
Because these pairs share no squares, a single guess can touch at most one of them. Thus any three guesses leave at least one of these four positions untouched.

This remains true even if later guesses depend on earlier replies. Follow the three guesses that the strategy makes when every reply is a miss. A rectangle occupying an untouched pair would give exactly those three misses. Therefore, three turns cannot guarantee success.

For a strategy that succeeds within four turns, color squares \(2,4,6,8\) black and the other five squares white. Adjacent squares have opposite colors, so every allowed rectangle covers one black square. Guessing the four black squares guarantees a hit.

The minimum is therefore \(\boxed{4}\) turns, choice \(\text{C}\).

solutions.title: Count positions ruled out
solutions.explanation:
To guarantee a hit, the guessed squares must meet every possible rectangle position. Counting how many positions three guesses can eliminate will show that three turns are insufficient.

Each row contains two horizontal positions, giving \(3\cdot2=6\). There are also \(6\) vertical positions, for \(12\) positions altogether.

For any strategy, consider its first three guesses when every reply is a miss. Separate these guesses into two cases.

- If the center is not guessed, each guessed square belongs to at most three rectangle positions: a corner has two neighboring squares, and a side-middle square has three. The three guesses therefore eliminate at most \(3\cdot3=9\) positions.
- If the center is guessed, first count the four positions containing it. Once those are removed, the remaining positions join consecutive squares along the outer border. Each other square belongs to at most two of these positions. The two other guesses therefore eliminate at most four additional positions, for at most \(4+2+2=8\) in total.

These are upper bounds because a position counted more than once is still eliminated only once. In either case, fewer than \(12\) positions are eliminated. A rectangle in a remaining position would produce all three misses, even when guesses depend on earlier replies.

Four turns suffice: guess the middle square on each of the four sides. Every horizontal or vertical adjacent pair contains exactly one of these four squares, so every possible rectangle is hit.

Thus the minimum is \(\boxed{4}\) turns, choice \(\text{C}\).
